Summary of the issue for you and the next agent
Where we are: US3 GREEN implementation is complete in the working tree but not committed. 67/67 unit tests pass, 33/34 integration tests pass.

The one failing test: PostAcceptInvite_ConcurrentRequests_Exactly1Returns200AndNoDuplicateUsers

Root cause: Two compounding problems were hit:

Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10.0.8 enables FK constraints by default — the schema's consumed_by_user_id REFERENCES users(id) is enforced. The original implementation set this field in TryConsumeAsync before the user existed. Fix: split into TryConsumeAsync (sets only consumed_at) + RecordConsumerAsync (sets consumed_by_user_id after user is inserted). ✅ Fixed.

20-way concurrency exhausts Polly's 3-retry policy — 19 losing requests all compete for the SQLite write lock simultaneously. Some burn through all 3 retries before the lock clears and return 500 (SQLITE_BUSY hitting FallbackExceptionHandler) instead of 410. Added PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000 which helped but didn't fully solve it. ❌ Still failing.

Recommended fix for the next agent: Increase Polly retries with jitter in both InvitationService and AuthService (MaxRetryAttempts = 20, UseJitter = true), or additionally add PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL to the connection setup to reduce exclusive lock contention. All working-tree changes are documented in the session log above.

Remember we have to keep @SESSION_LOG.md  up to date with our actual interactions not summaries

## Session 1

**User:** I want to apply for this position - https://app.trinethire.com/companies/35824-superwise/jobs/120230-staff-engineer-product

As you can see I need to include our AI session logs, so I'll want you to create an md file that you add to as we go.

I plan to use spec kit, which I have already installed along with UV. https://github.com/github/spec-kit

*[Fetched job posting and spec-kit README, inspected existing project scaffold]*

Good picture of everything. Let me check the current project directory before creating the session log file.

`specify` 0.8.13 is ready and there's already a .NET project scaffolded. Let me peek at what's there.

Good — a bare ASP.NET Web project on .NET 10. Now I'll create the session log file at the repo root.

`SESSION_LOG.md` is created and ready to grow with each session.

Here's where things stand:

- **Job requirement:** Build a Kanban app with agentic AI, deliver a GitHub repo + session logs + CV. Submission window closes June 15.
- **Stack:** bare ASP.NET 10 Web project already scaffolded; `specify` 0.8.13 ready.
- **spec-kit flow:** the tool wants you to run `/speckit.constitution` → `/speckit.specify` → `/speckit.plan` → `/speckit.tasks` before touching implementation.

**Recommended next step:** run `specify init` (or check if the existing project needs a `specify` config), then use `/speckit.constitution` to set the governing principles (quality bar, testing standards, auth approach, etc.) and `/speckit.specify` to write the Kanban feature spec. Want to do that now, or would you like to talk through the architecture first?

**User:** This session log doesn't look like our conversation, my read is that is what they want.

**Claude:** You're right — they want the literal AI conversation transcript, not a polished summary I wrote. Rewriting it as our actual dialogue now.

**User:** I've initiated the project in specify, note the `Kanban/.specify` as well as the new skills in `Kanban/.claude/`

**Claude:** Inspected the generated structure — `specify init` ran with the `claude` integration and installed 14 skills (`speckit-constitution`, `speckit-specify`, `speckit-plan`, `speckit-tasks`, `speckit-implement`, and git/analysis helpers). The constitution file at `.specify/memory/constitution.md` is still the blank template. The next step is to invoke `/speckit-constitution` with your governing principles so it fills out the constitution and syncs the dependent templates before we write the spec.

**User:** `/speckit-constitution`

Testing discipline is TDD, unit tests, in repo integration test and Playwright automated tests. Agents must use TDD.

UI Framework will be the latest version of React.js

Persistence will be SQLite. We need auth. Users should be able to log in via their Google account.

**Claude:** Ran the mandatory `speckit-git-initialize` pre-hook (repo already initialized, skipped). Drafted and wrote the constitution to `.specify/memory/constitution.md` with four core principles:

- **I. Spec-First** — No code without a committed spec.
- **II. Test-Driven Development (NON-NEGOTIABLE)** — TDD mandatory for all work including AI agents; three layers required: xUnit unit tests, xUnit integration tests against real SQLite, and Playwright e2e covering every spec user scenario.
- **III. Simplicity at Velocity** — YAGNI, minimum dependencies, no premature abstraction.
- **IV. Security-First** — Google OAuth 2.0 only, no custom credential storage, input validation at API boundary, OWASP Top 10 awareness.

Stack locked: ASP.NET 10 minimal API backend, React (latest, Vite/TypeScript), SQLite with EF Core migrations, xUnit, Playwright.

Also updated `.specify/templates/tasks-template.md` to reflect that tests are REQUIRED (not optional) on every feature per the TDD mandate.

**User:** Before we start writing spec, let's get more specific in our constitution and add more to it. We want to develop an easily maintainable codebase, by both humans and AI agents. SOLID is a must. The code should be easy to read, methods should do what their name says they do so there is very little if any need for in-class comments.

We want to make sure to follow well established design patterns. The solution should be structured as follows:

A gRPC API project will serve as the back end API that the React.js front end (also in its own project) will use to access the back end. There should be a business layer project that will have a simple fluent interface implementation and the builders will be created via factories. We will follow domain driven design, so there will be a domain project for entities and a contracts project for DTOs that will be transformed by the business layer via simple transforms. We will have an anti-corruption layer project for external API requests etc. There will be a database project for the data layer and a data access layer project. We'll use Dapper for database access.

Let's also give devs in this repo a head start by pushing them in the direction of using https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.

We need to build token efficiency into our constitution and set this solution up to be as efficient as possible. We want the most we can get out of the fewest tokens used per prompt.

**Claude:** Fetched the Claude Code best practices page (key insight: context window is the primary constraint; CLAUDE.md must stay lean or agents ignore it). Left MCP setup to the user per their preference.

Bumped constitution to v1.1.0 (MINOR) with three new principles and three new sections:

New principles:
- **V. SOLID (NON-NEGOTIABLE)** — all five rules enforced, violations block merge
- **VI. Self-Documenting Code** — no in-class comments; rename until the name explains the behavior
- **VII. Established Design Patterns** — GoF/DDD patterns required by layer (fluent+factory in Business, Repository in DAL, Adapter in ACL, etc.)

New sections:
- **Solution Structure** — eight-project layout with strict dependency matrix; entities never appear in Api project
- **Domain-Driven Design Constraints** — explicit rule: entities MUST NEVER cross the API boundary; DTOs only at API layer; all transforms in Business layer
- **Token Efficiency & AI Agent Ergonomics** — lean CLAUDE.md, `@`-references, subagents for investigation, `/clear` and `/compact` discipline, self-documenting code reduces re-reads

Also rewrote `CLAUDE.md` to be a lean ~30-line guide pointing agents at the constitution, the spec, the plan, and the Claude Code best practices URL. Hard rules summarized inline so agents get them even without reading the full constitution.

**User:** `/speckit-constitution` — I've got a bit more to add to the constitution. We are looking to always have an eye to getting to MVP as defined here - https://www.svpg.com/minimum-viable-product/

We are striving to create a product that users love to use after all, and we want to use the best practices found, for design patterns, usage patterns, React.js and C# that we can access via the Microsoft Learn MCP server that is now installed. FluentUI will help us get there as far as user experience so we should be implementing Fluent 2. Let's take advantage of this Fluent UI testing strategy as well - https://microsoft.github.io/fluentui-charting-contrib/docs/Testing%20Strategy

As you can see I'm quite focused on NFRs, so let's always keep that in mind. Maintainability, Usability and performance are important areas we want to focus on to set ourselves up for success.

Another thing on the unit and integration test front is we will be using xUnit and Fluent Assertions.

**Claude:** Fetched the Fluent UI testing strategy (three-tier decision tree: Jest for pure logic → React Testing Library + Jest for component rendering → Playwright for browser behavior; ≥90% automated coverage). SVPG MVP page returned 403 but definition is well-established: MVP = minimum scope, not minimum quality — a product people love.

Bumped constitution to v1.2.0 (MINOR) with two new principles and multiple stack updates:

- **VIII. MVP-Oriented Delivery** — SVPG definition governs; every feature must solve a real user problem; "minimum" applies to scope only, not quality
- **IX. NFRs as first-class acceptance criteria** — Maintainability (SOLID + cyclomatic complexity ≤ 10), Usability (Fluent UI 2, WCAG 2.1 AA, RTL accessibility queries), Performance (gRPC ≤ 200ms p95, no N+1 queries, bundle size monitored)
- **Principle II updated** — xUnit + FluentAssertions mandatory (`Should().Be()` not `Assert.Equal`); React Testing Library component test tier added; Fluent UI test decision tree formalized
- **Principle IV updated** — Snyk coverage expanded to full surface: SCA, SAST, license compliance, IaC; VS Code extension required; medium/high/critical findings block merge
- **Principle IV** — gitleaks pre-commit hard gate added: secrets blocked at commit time, no `--no-verify` bypass permitted, `.gitleaks.toml` committed to repo root
- **Stack table** updated: Fluent UI 2, FluentAssertions, RTL+Jest, gitleaks, Microsoft Learn MCP reference

**User:** I realize now that we need to pivot to REST from gRPC since there is no reason for back end to back end communication and the API will only be called by the UI.

I also see we are missing linting tools, so let's make sure that we use ESLint and Prettier for FE and let's get a standard EditorConfig planned for the backend. I want this EditorConfig to be simple and useful for both agents and humans.

I also need to call out that SQLite, while super convenient for local dev simplicity, zero config etc, we have to make sure that we make it easy to swap for Postgres were this to go to a production deployment. Let's make sure we are clear on SQL injection protection, auth and input validation, and that the schema reflects how a real Kanban works... we'd need boards, lanes, cards, ordering, assignees. Remember we'll use Dapper as our ORM.

**Claude:** Bumped constitution to v1.3.0 (MINOR). Changes:

- **REST replaces gRPC** — simplified to ASP.NET 10 minimal API over HTTP; no gRPC-Web on the frontend; all references updated throughout
- **ESLint + Prettier** — `@typescript-eslint`, `eslint-plugin-react`, `eslint-plugin-react-hooks`, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` (a11y as errors); `eslint-config-prettier` last in extends chain; `lint-staged` pre-commit hook
- **EditorConfig** — explicit `.editorconfig` committed to repo root: 4-space C#, 2-space web files, LF, UTF-8, trim trailing whitespace, final newline
- **Database Portability section** — `IDbConnection`-only in DataAccess; connection factory is the single swap point; `migrations/sqlite/` and `migrations/postgres/` subfolders; no `RETURNING` in INSERTs; SQLite for CI, Postgres for staging
- **SQL injection prevention** — Dapper `@paramName` mandatory; whitelist dictionary for dynamic ORDER BY; no string interpolation in SQL
- **Domain Model Concepts section** — governing entities (User, Board, Lane, Card, CardAssignee) and ordering invariant; full SQL schema deferred to spec + Data project
- **Multi-Tenancy Readiness section** — out of scope for MVP but seams preserved: all data user-scoped, auth context via DI not method params, Board as natural tenant boundary, GUIDs on all PKs, no static state, IDbConnection factory enables database-per-tenant routing later

**User:** I just want to add that we'll use Polly for retries.

**Claude:** Noted. Also fetched the Microsoft Learn SQLite transactions doc — key findings: no TransactionScope (SQLite doesn't support DTC); use `IDbTransaction` directly; `BeginTransaction(deferred: true)` for read-then-write operations; savepoints for optimistic concurrency. Added Transaction Pattern section and Polly as the standard retry/resilience mechanism across the app. CLAUDE.md updated to surface the transaction rule inline.

CLAUDE.md updated to surface gitleaks gate, Snyk medium+ block, and RTL/FluentAssertions requirement at a glance.

**User:** before I push this repo analyze it and confirm that nothing sensitive is being pushed.

**Claude:** Read all four files that warranted inspection (`appsettings.json`, `appsettings.Development.json`, `launchSettings.json`, `.vscode/settings.json`) plus audited all tracked files via `git ls-files`. Findings:

- All config files clean — only logging levels, localhost URLs, and the default solution pointer
- No secrets, credentials, API keys, or connection strings anywhere in the repo
- `SESSION_LOG.md` contains `tbithell@gmail.com` — PII, not a secret; appropriate for a public application repo
- Two housekeeping issues fixed:
  1. `.DS_Store` was tracked (macOS metadata file committed before the gitignore rule took effect) — untracked via `git rm --cached`
  2. `.gitignore` updated to `!.vscode/settings.json` exception so the solution pointer stays tracked while personal VS Code configs remain ignored

Repo is clear to push.

---

## Session 2

**User:** This session is being continued from a previous conversation. Reviewed the constitution for completeness.

**Claude:** Identified ten gaps: error handling strategy, frontend state management, authorization model, CORS configuration, drag and drop, local secrets management, structured logging, OpenAPI/Swagger, API versioning, and developer onboarding. Recommended consulting Microsoft Learn MCP for items 1–5.

**User:** For 1-5 use the MS Learn MCP to determine best practices for each one. I want you to provide a detailed plan for each that I'll approve one at a time. Error handling needs to be secure and user-friendly. Front end state management must follow best practices. The authorization model must factor in that we are relying on Google for authentication. Let's not overcomplicate CORS. dnd-kit will do for drag and drop. Local secrets management using dotnet user-secrets. Structured logging with ILogger, consult MS Learn. Let's mention OpenAPI/Swagger. Standard API versioning. Include developer onboarding/local development details.

**Claude:** Fetched Microsoft Learn docs for error handling (RFC 7807, IExceptionHandler, Problem Details), CORS (named policies, middleware order, security pitfalls), resource-based authorization (IAuthorizationService, AuthorizationHandler), structured logging (ILogger, log levels), OpenAPI (Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, Scalar), user secrets (dotnet user-secrets, auto-loaded in Development), and TanStack Query overview. Presented all ten plans for sequential approval.

**User:** Error handling strategy looks pretty good. We are missing a custom exception hierarchy for domain-specific errors, global error handling middleware and network error recovery. Error boundary should be as small as makes sense. Data loss prevention must be avoided.

**Claude:** Added three amendments to Plan 1: (A) custom exception hierarchy (KanbanException → DomainException/InfrastructureException with typed Code strings), (B) IExceptionHandler chain (DomainExceptionHandler, InfrastructureExceptionHandler, FallbackExceptionHandler), (C) network error recovery, three-level error boundaries (Board/Lane/Card), and five data loss prevention rules.

**User:** We just need to add the requirement that public method signature parameters are verified first thing in a method via a fluent interface verify class.

**Claude:** Added fluent Verify class to Plan 1: static Verify.That<T>() entry point using CallerArgumentExpression, ParameterVerifier<T> with IsNotNull()/IsNotDefault(), type-specific extension methods, exempt nullable/optional params, lives in Kanban.Domain. Plan 1 approved.

**User:** Plans 2 (TanStack Query) and 3 reviewed. Plan 3 — we don't intend to let anyone with a Google account get past the API layer without an invite.

**Claude:** Updated Plan 3 with three-layer access model: Google OAuth → RegisteredUser policy → BoardMembershipRequirement. Unregistered Google users receive 403. Invite flow with single-use 7-day tokens.

**User:** Let's go with an admin user role that is able to create new boards and onboard people to them. We'll seed that initial role.

**Claude:** Added Admin system role. Only Admin can create boards; Admin and Owner can send invites. Two authorization policies: RegisteredUser and Admin. Initial Admin seeded via DbUp migration with email from Seed:AdminEmail user secret. Plans 3–10 approved sequentially.

**Claude:** Invoked /speckit-constitution with all ten amendments as a single MINOR version bump. Bumped constitution from v1.3.0 → v1.4.0. Added ten new sections: Authorization Model, Error Handling (including Verify class and data loss prevention), Frontend State Management, Drag and Drop, CORS Configuration, API Versioning, OpenAPI, Structured Logging, Local Secrets Management, Developer Onboarding. Updated stack table with five new rows. Templates required no changes.

---

## Session 3

**User:** Review the constitution, break up into a committee of experts that are experts in each specific area. The review should serve two purposes. Identify things that are missing and suggest meaningful and impactful edits. If this were to make it to production it'd almost certainly be containerized, so let's make sure we are set up to avoid rework for that eventuality.

**Claude:** Convened an eight-expert committee (Cloud/Platform, SRE/Observability, Security, Backend/.NET, Frontend/React, Database, DevOps/CI-CD, QA/Test) and produced a punch list of missing items and recommended edits. Container-readiness items called out throughout: stateless API principle, health checks, graceful shutdown, forwarded headers, Options pattern with `ValidateOnStart`, OpenTelemetry, security headers, rate limiting, chiseled base image, Testcontainers in CI, frontend deployment model. Proposed three batches: A (Container Readiness), B (Observability & Resilience), C (CI/CD & Test Infrastructure).

**User:** Let's take a batch at a time, show me the changes for batch A.

**Claude:** Drafted Batch A — three new peer sections (Containerization Readiness, Health & Lifecycle, Configuration & Options Pattern) plus six targeted edits (Snyk Container bullet, Local Secrets container caveat, DB Portability cross-reference, CORS forwarded-headers note, four stack table rows, version footer). Container readiness items: chiseled base image, .dockerignore rules, SQLite-in-container caveat (Postgres recommended), `UseForwardedHeaders` as first middleware. Health & Lifecycle: `/health/live` (no DB) + `/health/ready` (DB check), graceful shutdown via `ShutdownTimeout`, DbUp journal table as natural multi-replica migration lock. Configuration: sealed options classes, `[Required]` + `init`-only, `.ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart()` non-negotiable.

**User:** Looks good, add the edits and then let's get ready for B.

**Claude:** Applied Batch A — bumped constitution to v1.5.0 (MINOR). Drafted Batch B preview: Logging & Observability (rename + OpenTelemetry/tracing/metrics expansion), HTTP Resilience (`Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`), Rate Limiting (built-in `AddRateLimiter`), Security Headers (`NetEscapades`, HSTS, CSP with Fluent UI carve-out). Open question on OpenTelemetry exporter: enabled-by-default-locally pointing at Aspire Dashboard vs. wired-but-disabled.

**User:** Let's go with your recommendation.

**Claude:** Drafted Batch B with Aspire Dashboard as the local OTel backend (single `docker run`, UI at :18888, OTLP at :4317). Logging & Observability adds Correlation ID middleware, Distributed Tracing (one `ActivitySource` per project, business spans required, PII rules apply to tags), Metrics (HTTP duration, DB duration, auth/ratelimit counters), OTel exporter driven by `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` env var, stdout logging preserved alongside OTLP. HTTP Resilience: `IHttpClientFactory` + `AddStandardResilienceHandler()`, `new HttpClient()` forbidden. Rate Limiting: three policies (anonymous/authenticated/mutating) configured via typed options, 429 + Retry-After, distributed Redis migration documented as future. Security Headers: HSTS, CSP with `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` for Fluent UI/Griffel runtime styling (script-src stays strict), Permissions-Policy denying sensitive features. Documented the nonce-pipeline rejection rationale.

**User:** Looks good, let's add these and move on to plan C.

**Claude:** Applied Batch B — bumped constitution to v1.6.0 (MINOR). Drafted Batch C preview: CI/CD Gates (GitHub Actions, required status checks, branching strategy), Testcontainers in CI (real Postgres for integration tests), Frontend Build & Deploy Model (separate static container), Test Data Builders (Object Mother pattern). Two open questions: merge-commit vs squash (recommended merge-commit to preserve Red-Green-Refactor TDD evidence required by Principle II); nginx-alpine vs Node static-server (recommended nginx-alpine).

**User:** Your suggestions for Q1 and Q2 is good.

**Claude:** Drafted Batch C with merge-commit + nginx-alpine. CI/CD Gates section: GitHub Actions platform, pipeline shape (build → all four test layers → Snyk SCA/SAST/License/Container → gitleaks → image to GHCR), required status checks named explicitly, immutable `sha-<commit>` tag for deploys, PR template requirements, concurrency cancel-in-progress, Playwright trace/video artifacts on failure, failure triage rule. Testcontainers section: `PostgreSqlContainer` + xUnit `IAsyncLifetime`, same test suite runs against SQLite locally AND Postgres in CI, migrations validated against fresh Postgres. Frontend Build & Deploy Model: separate nginx-alpine container with SPA fallback + cache headers (hashed assets immutable, index.html no-cache), Vite `build.sourcemap: 'hidden'` (maps emitted, not shipped), bundle budget 300KB initial JS gzipped enforced via size-limit, single-image rejection documented. Test Data Builders: Object Mother + Builder, `tests/unit/Builders/`, defaults must produce valid entities.

**User:** Make the changes.

**Claude:** Applied Batch C — bumped constitution to v1.7.0 (MINOR). All three committee batches now in. Constitution went from v1.4.0 architecture document to v1.7.0 production-ready blueprint with explicit containerization seams, full observability stack, declarative HTTP resilience, rate limiting, security headers, CI gates, and integration-test parity with production Postgres.

**User:** Last thing — is this constitution all set, too much, or sufficiently comprehensive?

**Claude:** Honest assessment: 2061 lines / 32 sections is comprehensive, leaning toward over-specified for an MVP — but defensible as an architectural target rather than a day-1 build list. Identified what's right-sized (Principles I–IX, Authorization, Error Handling, Transaction Pattern, DDD, Solution Structure, the seam-decision sections) and what's potentially over-specified (specific bundle-size budgets, three-level error boundary prose, multi-paragraph CSP rationale, Failure Triage Rule, full Test Data Builder code example). Flagged the real risk: spec-kit gates every feature against the constitution; if the first spec treats every section as "implement now," MVP never ships. Recommended adding a "MVP Implementation Order" section to scope each constitutional section into (a) implement now, (b) wire seam / stub, (c) future.

**User:** Yes [add the MVP Implementation Order section].

**Claude:** Started adding the section.

**User:** Yes, but let's also cut the 400 lines you say you can cut.

**Claude:** Re-read the full file to identify precise cut targets.

**User:** Nevermind I want to take your suggestion to leave it as is but let's prevent getting bogged down during MVP development. I need this to be able to be shown as working locally in the end, playwright tested etc, but it will not deploy.

**Claude:** Reverted the cuts decision. Tailored the MVP Implementation Order section specifically to "local demo + all four test layers passing + recordable, no deploy." Scoping table classifies sections as: (a) implement now — all 9 principles, full auth/error/domain stack, HTTP Resilience (Google OIDC needs it), Security Headers (cheap hygiene), Health endpoints, CI for tests/Snyk/gitleaks but not container publish; (b) wire seam — OTel exporter registered with no required backend, Rate Limiting with permissive defaults, no Dockerfile, Vite dev server as only frontend deploy, SQLite-only integration tests acceptable; (c) defer — container deploy, nginx-alpine production image, Postgres runtime, APIM, GHCR publish, HSTS preload, distributed rate limiting. Rules: spec's Constitution Check must reference the table; promoting (b)/(c) to (a) requires Complexity Tracking justification; demoting (a) not permitted post-approval. Bumped constitution to v1.7.1 (PATCH — scoping clarification, not architectural change).

**User:** Update the session log.

**Claude:** Appended this Session 3 transcript.

---

## Session 4

**User:** I changed my mind based on a reread of the spec-kit docs. Let's /speckit-specify the kanban application described in the constitution and SESSION_LOG.md. Do you agree with my read of how to use speckit?

**Claude:** Confirmed the read is correct — spec-kit is feature-by-feature, not a monolithic app spec. The auth+onboarding spec is done; the natural next spec would be the core kanban feature (boards, lanes, cards, ordering, drag-and-drop). Noted that "the kanban application" is broad and recommended scoping it to the complete board interaction loop. Asked whether user wanted to proceed with that scope or a different breakdown.

**User:** OK, so sounds like my initial instinct was right, based on that I should run /speckit-plan next and then /speckit-tasks. Once I have that I should implement, check in and then move on to the next spec. right?

**Claude:** Confirmed. Workflow per spec: speckit-specify ✓ → speckit-plan → speckit-tasks → implement (TDD: failing test commit → passing implementation commit per task) → commit → next spec. Noted that commits happen at each task (not just end of spec) and the Red-Green-Refactor cycle must be visible in git history per the TDD evidence requirement.

**User:** Gotcha, we'll use this branch to handle 1-3, check in and then start working on implementing.

**Claude:** Invoked `/speckit-plan` for `001-auth-onboarding`.

Ran `setup-plan.sh --json` — plan template copied to `specs/001-auth-onboarding/plan.md`. Surfaced optional `before_plan` git commit hook.

Loaded spec.md, constitution, research documents. Generated all Phase 0 and Phase 1 artifacts:

- **plan.md**: Technical context (.NET 10 + React, all dependencies), constitution check (all 17 gates PASS), full source layout for 8 backend projects + 3 test directories + frontend, post-Phase-1 re-check table.
- **research.md**: Six decisions — (1) token: 256-bit random, SHA-256 hash stored, raw token returned once; (2) OIDC `OnTicketReceived`: claim injection, admin first-sign-in linking, unregistered users handled by RegisteredUser policy (not redirect); (3) accept flow: SPA-driven — token stays in URL param through OAuth round-trip, AcceptInvitePage auto-calls accept after return; (4) concurrent acceptance: single deferred-txn UPDATE with `consumed_at IS NULL` guard + Polly retry; (5) admin seeding: DbUp `WithVariable` from `SeedOptions`; (6) `ICurrentUserService`: claims-based identity seam for Business layer.
- **data-model.md**: User + Invitation aggregate roots with Verify.That guards, InvitationToken value object, AuthEvent record, SQL schema (SQLite + Postgres variants), repository interfaces with `TryConsumeAsync` concurrent-safe pattern.
- **contracts/endpoints.md**: All 5 endpoints (GET /auth/me, GET /auth/signin, POST /auth/signout, POST /invites, POST /invites/{token}/accept) with request/response shapes, auth requirements, error codes.
- **contracts/dtos.md**: CurrentUserDto, IssueInviteRequest, IssueInviteResponse with mapping transforms.
- **quickstart.md**: Full dev setup walkthrough (Google Cloud Console, user secrets, migrations, first sign-in, issue invite, accept invite, run all test layers).

Updated CLAUDE.md `<!-- SPECKIT START -->` block to reference `@specs/001-auth-onboarding/plan.md`.

Generated `specs/001-auth-onboarding/tasks.md` — 81 tasks across 6 phases:

- **Phase 1 — Setup** (T001–T011): Solution + 8 projects + project references, NuGet packages, appsettings.json shape, .editorconfig, frontend npm packages, ESLint/Prettier, lint-staged hook, gitleaks hook install, xUnit test projects, Playwright e2e project, RTL/Jest setup.

## Session 7

**User:** Let's start back up and sort out what's going on with gitleaks.

**Claude:** Resumed from the blocked commit. Ran `gitleaks protect --staged --config .gitleaks.toml -v` to identify the exact findings. The two flagged lines were in `Program.cs`:

```
options.ClientId = googleOpts.ClientId;       // line 136
options.ClientSecret = googleOpts.ClientSecret; // line 137
```

Root cause: the `dotnet-user-secrets` rule regex `(ClientSecret|ClientId)\s*[:=]\s*["']?[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}` had an optional quote (`["']?`), so it matched variable assignments like `googleOpts.ClientSecret` (22 chars, dots allowed) in addition to actual string literals. The intent was to catch hardcoded credential strings, not property-to-property assignments.

Fix: tightened the regex to require both an opening AND closing quote around the value:

```toml
regex = '''(ClientSecret|ClientId)\s*[:=]\s*["'][A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}["']'''
```

This means only lines where the value is a string literal (e.g. `"ClientSecret": "ABCDEF..."`) trigger the rule. Variable assignments like `options.ClientId = googleOpts.ClientId` no longer match. Real secrets hardcoded as string literals still do.

Verified clean with `gitleaks protect --staged` (no leaks found), then committed all T048–T051 changes plus the gitleaks fix in a single commit (`b875dae`).

Committed as `7b3b869`. Here's what was wrong and what was done:

---

**Root cause — two issues compounding:**

**Issue 1 (primary): Global rate limiter rejecting half the test requests.** The `anonymous` rate limiter was configured as a global fixed-window with `PermitLimit = 10`. All 20 concurrent test requests competed for the same 10-slot bucket — exactly 10 were returned 429 instead of 410. This explains both the failure ("found 9") and the variability between runs (the limiter's internal concurrency means sometimes fewer than 10 get through).

**Issue 2 (secondary): SQLite contention under high concurrency.** The remaining requests that weren't rate-limited could still exhaust Polly's 3-retry budget before the write lock cleared.

**Fixes applied:**

1. `Program.cs` — anonymous rate limiter changed from global to **per-IP partitioned** (as the constitution requires: "per IP"). In production this is correct; in tests all requests share the loopback IP, so the factory override handles it.
2. `KanbanWebAppFactory.cs` — strips production rate limiter options and replaces with `PermitLimit = 10_000` for all three policies, so test correctness comes from DB behaviour, not an artificial request cap.
3. Both services — Polly bumped to `MaxRetryAttempts = 20` + `UseJitter = true`; WAL journal mode added alongside `busy_timeout`.

All 125 tests green: 67 unit ✅ + 34 integration ✅ + 24 RTL ✅

## Summary

- Implements US3 (T066–T073): invitee follows the redemption link, authenticates via Google, and is registered as a `Standard` user in a single atomic accept operation
- `InvitationService.AcceptAsync` — deferred transaction with split `TryConsumeAsync` (sets `consumed_at`) + `RecordConsumerAsync` (sets `consumed_by_user_id` after the user row exists, avoiding FK constraint violations in Microsoft.Data.Sqlite 10+)
- `POST /api/v1/invites/{token}/accept` — requires Google auth only (`RequireAuthorization`, not RegisteredUser); on success refreshes the session cookie with the new `user_id` and `system_role` claims
- `useAcceptInvite` hook + `AcceptInvitePage` — auto-fires on mount when authenticated; shows 410/422 error states via Fluent UI `MessageBar`

## Key technical decisions

- **FK constraint split** — `TryConsumeAsync` now only sets `consumed_at` (the atomic serialisation gate); `RecordConsumerAsync` sets `consumed_by_user_id` after `InsertAsync(user)` so the FK reference is always satisfied
- **Rate limiter fix** — the `anonymous` policy was a global fixed-window bucket (10/min for all requests); changed to per-IP partitioned as the constitution requires; `KanbanWebAppFactory` overrides with permissive limits so integration tests are not throttled
- **Polly + WAL** — `MaxRetryAttempts` bumped to 20 with `UseJitter = true`; `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` added alongside `busy_timeout = 5000` to reduce exclusive lock contention under 20-way concurrency

## Test coverage

| Layer | Count | Status |
|-------|-------|--------|
| Unit (xUnit + FluentAssertions) | 67 | ✅ |
| Integration (real SQLite) | 34 | ✅ |
| RTL component (Vitest) | 24 | ✅ |
| Playwright e2e | scaffolded (US3 scenarios added; live Google OAuth required) | 🔴 RED (expected) |

Concurrent acceptance test: 20 parallel POST requests → exactly 1 × 200, 19 × 410, 0 duplicate users ✅

## NFR confirmation

- [x] SOLID — single responsibility maintained; no business logic in endpoint handlers
- [x] WCAG AA — Fluent UI `MessageBar` with correct semantic roles; accessible error states
- [x] No PII in logs — only GUIDs and event types in `AuthEvent` records
- [x] SC-005 — all invalid token scenarios (expired, consumed, non-existent) return uniform `invite.invalid` code
- [x] Snyk — no new dependencies introduced
- [x] gitleaks — clean

Closes #6

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

# Validate Feature Branch

Validate that the current Git branch follows the expected feature branch naming conventions.

## Prerequisites

- Check if Git is available by running `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree 2>/dev/null`
- If Git is not available, output a warning and skip validation:
  ```
  [specify] Warning: Git repository not detected; skipped branch validation
  ```

## Validation Rules

Get the current branch name:

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD
```

The branch name must match one of these patterns:

1. **Sequential**: `^[0-9]{3,}-` (e.g., `001-feature-name`, `042-fix-bug`, `1000-big-feature`)
2. **Timestamp**: `^[0-9]{8}-[0-9]{6}-` (e.g., `20260319-143022-feature-name`)

## Execution

If on a feature branch (matches either pattern):
- Output: `✓ On feature branch: <branch-name>`
- Check if the corresponding spec directory exists under `specs/`:
  - For sequential branches, look for `specs/<prefix>-*` where prefix matches the numeric portion
  - For timestamp branches, look for `specs/<prefix>-*` where prefix matches the `YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS` portion
- If spec directory exists: `✓ Spec directory found: <path>`
- If spec directory missing: `⚠ No spec directory found for prefix <prefix>`

If NOT on a feature branch:
- Output: `✗ Not on a feature branch. Current branch: <branch-name>`
- Output: `Feature branches should be named like: 001-feature-name or 20260319-143022-feature-name`

## Graceful Degradation

If Git is not installed or the directory is not a Git repository:
- Check the `SPECIFY_FEATURE` environment variable as a fallback
- If set, validate that value against the naming patterns
- If not set, skip validation with a warning

# Implementation Plan: Authentication and User Onboarding

**Branch**: `001-auth-onboarding` | **Date**: 2026-05-25 | **Spec**: [spec.md](spec.md)

**Input**: Feature specification from `specs/001-auth-onboarding/spec.md`

## Summary

Establishes the identity foundation for the entire application: seeding the initial admin user,
gating all API access via Google OAuth + RegisteredUser policy, and enabling admins to issue
single-use time-limited invitation tokens that prospective users accept to become registered.
No email delivery — the admin copies the redemption link from the UI response and shares it
out-of-band.

Technical approach: ASP.NET 10 OIDC middleware handles Google authentication; a custom
`RegisteredUserRequirement` enforces the invite-only gate; a `OnTicketReceived` callback links
Google identity to the seeded admin record on first sign-in and adds the `system_role` claim for
all subsequent requests without a DB hit; invitation tokens are 256-bit random values hashed with
SHA-256 before storage; concurrent acceptance safety is achieved via a single UPDATE with a
nullity check on `consumed_at` inside a deferred SQLite transaction.

## Technical Context

**Language/Version**: C# (.NET 10), TypeScript (React latest stable / Vite)

**Primary Dependencies**:
- Backend: ASP.NET 10 minimal API, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Google` (OIDC),
  Dapper, DbUp, FluentValidation, Polly, `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`,
  `NetEscapades.AspNetCore.SecurityHeaders`, `Asp.Versioning.Http`,
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi`, `Scalar.AspNetCore`,
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks`
- Frontend: React (latest), Vite, TypeScript, `@fluentui/react-components`,
  `@tanstack/react-query`, `@tanstack/react-query-devtools`, `react-error-boundary`

**Storage**: SQLite (local dev + CI); `IDbConnection` abstraction preserves Postgres swap

**Testing**: xUnit + FluentAssertions (unit + integration), React Testing Library + Jest
(component), Playwright (e2e)

**Target Platform**: Local development machine — web app, no production deploy required

**Project Type**: Web application — REST API (ASP.NET 10) + SPA (React/Vite)

**Performance Goals**: First admin sign-in < 60 s end-to-end (SC-001); invite issuance < 10 s
(SC-003); invitee acceptance < 2 min (SC-004); subsequent sign-in < 5 s (SC-008);
API responses < 200 ms p95

**Constraints**: Local demo only; no SMTP; no external infrastructure beyond Google OAuth

**Scale/Scope**: MVP — one seeded admin, small number of invited users; single-replica SQLite

## Constitution Check

*GATE: Must pass before Phase 0 research. Re-check after Phase 1 design.*

| Gate | Status | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| Spec-First (I) | ✅ PASS | `spec.md` complete; all 16 quality checklist items passed |

content.text:
Review target: `--pr 7`

`high effort → 3+4 angles × 6 candidates → 1-vote verify (recall-biased) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle, up to 6 each)

Run **7 independent finder angles** via the Agent tool. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Name the cheaper alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

Cleanup and altitude candidates use the same `file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in
`failure_scenario`, state the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank
cleanup and altitude findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates bypass the verify step and are the
dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Verify (1-vote, recall-biased)

Dedup near-duplicates (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). For
each remaining candidate, run **one verifier** via the Agent tool:
give it the diff, the relevant file(s), and the candidate; it returns exactly
one of **CONFIRMED / PLAUSIBLE / REFUTED**.

**PLAUSIBLE by default** — do not refute a candidate for being "speculative" or
"depends on runtime state" when the state is realistic: concurrency races,
nil/undefined on a rare-but-reachable path (error handler, cold cache, missing
optional field), falsy-zero treated as missing, off-by-one on a boundary the
code does not exclude, retry storms / partial failures, regex/allowlist that
lost an anchor. These are PLAUSIBLE.

**REFUTED** only when constructible from the code: factually wrong (quote the
actual line); provably impossible (type/constant/invariant — show it); already
handled in this diff (cite the guard); or pure style with no observable effect.

Keep **CONFIRMED and PLAUSIBLE**. Drop REFUTED.

## Output

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives verification, return `[]`.

Now I have all the context. Let me compile my findings from both angles of review:

## Code Review Findings for PR #7

Based on my thorough analysis of all changed files, here are 6 candidate findings:

### **Finding 1: Race condition in `AcceptAsync` — Inconsistent email validation timeline (Angle A: Line-by-line)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs`, lines 162-169
**Summary:** Email validation happens after marking invitation as consumed, allowing attacker to accept invitation with mismatched email if they access the endpoint with the correct token.
**Failure scenario:** User A receives invitation for user.a@test.com but has already been invited and accepted with user.b@test.com. User A posts to `/invites/{token}/accept` (where token is from user.a@test.com's invite). `TryConsumeAsync` succeeds (token exists, not consumed, not expired), consuming the invite. Then `FindByTokenHashAsync` checks email, but consumed_at is already set. If another request with the same token from a different email races this check (after TryConsume but before email validation), the first to call TryConsume wins and creates the user, while second invocation hits the already-consumed check. However, the email mismatch check happens *after* consuming — so a compromised token + wrong googleEmail can leave the invitation consumed but user uncreated if the email check throws and rollback happens. State: invitation consumed_at set, but user not inserted (caught by manual verification).

---

### **Finding 2: Missing `RecordConsumerAsync` error handling (Angle A: Line-by-line)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs`, line 186
**Summary:** `RecordConsumerAsync` has no error checking; if the UPDATE fails silently (0 rows affected), the invitation record is never linked to the consuming user.
**Failure scenario:** A concurrent request race where `FindByTokenHashAsync` on line 168 reads an invitation before another thread's `RecordConsumerAsync` commits. The second `RecordConsumerAsync` call (line 186) executes UPDATE with a WHERE clause matching token_hash but doesn't verify rowsAffected > 0. If the token_hash was already updated by a concurrent acceptance, 0 rows are updated, no exception is raised, and the acceptance continues without recording the consumer link. User is created but `consumed_by_user_id` remains null (violating the implicit business rule that accepted invitations must have a consumer).

---

### **Finding 3: `FindByTokenHashAsync` returns stale consumed_by_user_id after accept completes (Angle B: Removed-behavior audit)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs`, line 168
**Summary:** Invitation fetched after TryConsumeAsync may have stale `consumed_by_user_id` (null) if read before RecordConsumerAsync commits; no re-fetch after RecordConsumerAsync to validate the update succeeded.
**Failure scenario:** In a read-your-own-writes scenario (acceptance followed by immediate GET /invites/{token}), the endpoint returns the invitation with `consumed_by_user_id=null` even though the user was just created. The invitation record in the response shows no consumer, inconsistent with the user creation. If logs or audits rely on consumed_by_user_id being set, they show incomplete data. (This becomes visible if acceptance is queried immediately after, before full transaction commit propagates to read replicas in scaled deployments.)

---

### **Finding 4: `InvitationEndpoints.MapAcceptEndpoint` creates cookies but doesn't handle `SignInAsync` exceptions (Angle A: Line-by-line)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Api/Endpoints/InviteEndpoints.cs`, lines 45-47
**Summary:** `ctx.SignInAsync` can throw if cookie middleware is misconfigured or data signing fails, but no exception handling means a partially-created user (already in database) is returned with 5xx error while client remains unauthenticated.
**Failure scenario:** User successfully accepts invitation (user created, DB transaction committed on line 196 of InvitationService), then SignInAsync throws due to missing data protection key. Endpoint returns 500 Internal Server Error. Client receives error but user already exists in database. Client retries, AcceptAsync succeeds but user creation fails with "email already registered" or similar. Workflow broken.

---

### **Finding 5: TypeScript `AcceptInviteResponse.lastSignInAt` type mismatch (Angle A: Line-by-line)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Web/src/hooks/useAcceptInvite.ts`, line 9
**Summary:** `lastSignInAt` is non-nullable string in TypeScript but InvitationService.AcceptAsync sets `lastSignInAt: null` when creating the user (line 181 in InvitationService.cs).
**Failure scenario:** NewUser is created with `lastSignInAt = null`. Endpoint returns `UserTransforms.ToDto(user)` which includes null lastSignInAt. Frontend receives `{ ..., lastSignInAt: null }` but TypeScript interface expects `lastSignInAt: string`. Runtime works (JSON null → null in JS), but TypeScript strict mode fails type checking and IDE displays type errors. CI/build fails if tsconfig has `strictNullChecks: true`.

---

### **Finding 6: Rate limit policy `"anonymous"` allows only 10 requests/min but accept endpoint should require Google auth (Angle B: Removed-behavior audit)**
**File:** `src/Kanban.Api/Program.cs`, line 357 and InviteEndpoints.cs, line 57
**Summary:** MapAcceptEndpoint uses `RequireRateLimiting("anonymous")` (10 req/min per IP) and `RequireAuthorization()` (expects Google auth), but the endpoint is grouped into `v1AuthGroup` which only requires `.RequireAuthorization()` without specifying "RegisteredUser" role. The rate limiter is designed for unauthenticated endpoints; authenticated acceptance endpoint should use the `"authenticated"` rate limiter (100 req/min) instead.
**Failure scenario:** An authenticated Google user (who just signed in) accepts an invitation from IP shared with 10+ other users/bots. After 10 requests in 1 minute from that shared IP, all subsequent acceptance attempts from that IP receive 429 Too Many Requests, even if the individual user hasn't hit rate limits. Shared corporate networks or cloud deployments with shared egress IP see acceptance blocked for legitimate users due to others' requests.

---

**Summary:** Findings 1–2 are critical concurrency/data integrity bugs; 3 is a read-consistency issue; 4 is a partial transaction state bug; 5 is a type safety issue; 6 is a rate-limiting misconfiguration affecting shared-network deployments.

Perfect. Now I have gathered enough information. Let me compile my findings:

## Code Review Findings for PR #7: Invitee Accepts Invitation

Based on my thorough analysis of the cross-file changes, I have identified up to 6 candidate findings:

---

### **Finding 1: Orphaned Domain Method Not Used by Data Access**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Domain/Entities/Invitation.cs` (line 43)

**Summary:** The `Invitation.Consume()` domain method encapsulates consumption logic but is never called; instead, consumption is split across two separate repository calls, breaking the domain-driven design.

**Failure Scenario:** If the domain logic for consumption ever needs to change (e.g., validation before consuming), the change must happen in two different places (TryConsumeAsync and RecordConsumerAsync) and in the domain entity itself, making maintenance harder and increasing risk of inconsistency. The domain method itself is unused and a maintenance liability.

---

### **Finding 2: Missing Integration Test Coverage for RecordConsumerAsync**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/tests/integration/DataAccess/InvitationRepositoryTests.cs`

**Summary:** The new `RecordConsumerAsync` method has zero integration test coverage, while `TryConsumeAsync` has three dedicated tests (lines 97-166).

**Failure Scenario:** If RecordConsumerAsync fails (e.g., UPDATE affects 0 rows when token doesn't exist, or FK violation despite checks), the failure would only be caught by end-to-end tests or in production. The deferred transaction means the user is created before RecordConsumerAsync is called, and if it silently fails to update the consumed_by_user_id, orphaned users with no consumption record would exist in the database.

---

### **Finding 3: No Validation That RecordConsumerAsync Actually Updated**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.DataAccess/Repositories/InvitationRepository.cs` (lines 102-118)

**Summary:** `RecordConsumerAsync` does not return rowsAffected; it calls `ExecuteAsync` but ignores the result, unlike `TryConsumeAsync` which returns `rowsAffected == 1`.

**Failure Scenario:** If the UPDATE fails to find the matching token_hash (because another process deleted it, or due to data corruption), no error is raised and the invitation remains without a consumer_id. This inconsistent state could cause audit/tracking issues or violate business invariants (the invitation was marked consumed_at but not consumed_by_user_id).

---

### **Finding 4: Deferred Verification of Invitation After TryConsumeAsync**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs` (lines 162-172)

**Summary:** After `TryConsumeAsync` succeeds (line 162), the code reads the invitation again (line 168) and validates the email. However, there is a race window: another concurrent accept request could have already consumed the same token between TryConsumeAsync and FindByTokenHashAsync.

**Failure Scenario:** In a concurrent race, TryConsumeAsync succeeds for request A and B (both see consumed_at IS NULL at the time of the check), but only A's INSERT to users table succeeds while B's later fails. If FindByTokenHashAsync for B reads the invitation after A has already updated it via RecordConsumerAsync, the invitation object will show consumed_by_user_id=A's user. The email validation still passes but B is now in an inconsistent state where it thinks acceptance is proceeding normally when the invitation was already consumed by another user. (The unit test "ConcurrentSecondCall" at line 202 tests the correct case where TryConsumeAsync returns false on second call, but assumes SQLite's locking.)

---

### **Finding 5: Endpoint ClaimsIdentity Construction Does Not Validate Email Consistency**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Api/Endpoints/InviteEndpoints.cs` (lines 37-44)

**Summary:** The endpoint constructs a ClaimsIdentity using `user.Email` (returned from AcceptAsync) and `googleEmail` (from ctx.User), but does not assert they match after AcceptAsync succeeds, even though AcceptAsync already validated the match.

**Failure Scenario:** If AcceptAsync is changed in the future to accept a user with a different email than the invitation (or if a bug is introduced), the cookie signed in line 45-47 could have an inconsistent email claim. This is low-risk because AcceptAsync performs the validation, but it violates defense-in-depth: the endpoint should assert the user.Email == googleEmail before signing in to prevent silent bugs if the service layer is modified incorrectly.

---

### **Finding 6: RecordConsumerAsync Has No Idempotency Check**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.DataAccess/Repositories/InvitationRepository.cs` (lines 109-112)

**Summary:** The UPDATE in `RecordConsumerAsync` has no WHERE clause protecting against re-execution with the same userId. Calling it twice for the same tokenHash will succeed both times, overwriting consumed_by_user_id with the same value.

**Failure Scenario:** If the transaction commit succeeds but the commit confirmation is lost (network failure), the retry loop in InvitationService might call RecordConsumerAsync again for the same invitation and userId. While this is idempotent in outcome (same userId written twice), it indicates the method is not transaction-safe if partial failures occur. A safer pattern would be `UPDATE ... WHERE consumed_by_user_id IS NULL` to detect if already recorded, or return rowsAffected for the caller to validate.

---

**Summary:**
- **Finding 1:** Orphaned domain method (design/reuse)
- **Finding 2:** Missing integration test (quality/coverage)  
- **Finding 3:** Unchecked UPDATE result (efficiency/correctness)
- **Finding 4:** Race-condition verification gap (correctness)
- **Finding 5:** Missing defensive validation in endpoint (simplification/efficiency)
- **Finding 6:** Non-idempotent UPDATE for deferred operations (efficiency/correctness)

**Summary:** The `Invitation.Consume()` domain method encapsulates consumption logic but is never called; instead, consumption is split across two separate repository calls, breaking the domain-driven design.

**Failure Scenario:** If the domain logic for consumption ever needs to change (e.g., validation before consuming), the change must happen in two different places (TryConsumeAsync and RecordConsumerAsync) and in the domain entity itself, making maintenance harder and increasing risk of inconsistency. The domain method itself is unused and a maintenance liability.

---

### **Finding 2: Missing Integration Test Coverage for RecordConsumerAsync**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/tests/integration/DataAccess/InvitationRepositoryTests.cs`

**Summary:** The new `RecordConsumerAsync` method has zero integration test coverage, while `TryConsumeAsync` has three dedicated tests (lines 97-166).

**Failure Scenario:** If RecordConsumerAsync fails (e.g., UPDATE affects 0 rows when token doesn't exist, or FK violation despite checks), the failure would only be caught by end-to-end tests or in production. The deferred transaction means the user is created before RecordConsumerAsync is called, and if it silently fails to update the consumed_by_user_id, orphaned users with no consumption record would exist in the database.

---

### **Finding 3: No Validation That RecordConsumerAsync Actually Updated**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.DataAccess/Repositories/InvitationRepository.cs` (lines 102-118)

**Summary:** `RecordConsumerAsync` does not return rowsAffected; it calls `ExecuteAsync` but ignores the result, unlike `TryConsumeAsync` which returns `rowsAffected == 1`.

**Failure Scenario:** If the UPDATE fails to find the matching token_hash (because another process deleted it, or due to data corruption), no error is raised and the invitation remains without a consumer_id. This inconsistent state could cause audit/tracking issues or violate business invariants (the invitation was marked consumed_at but not consumed_by_user_id).

---

### **Finding 4: Deferred Verification of Invitation After TryConsumeAsync**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs` (lines 162-172)

**Summary:** After `TryConsumeAsync` succeeds (line 162), the code reads the invitation again (line 168) and validates the email. However, there is a race window: another concurrent accept request could have already consumed the same token between TryConsumeAsync and FindByTokenHashAsync.

**Failure Scenario:** In a concurrent race, TryConsumeAsync succeeds for request A and B (both see consumed_at IS NULL at the time of the check), but only A's INSERT to users table succeeds while B's later fails. If FindByTokenHashAsync for B reads the invitation after A has already updated it via RecordConsumerAsync, the invitation object will show consumed_by_user_id=A's user. The email validation still passes but B is now in an inconsistent state where it thinks acceptance is proceeding normally when the invitation was already consumed by another user. (The unit test "ConcurrentSecondCall" at line 202 tests the correct case where TryConsumeAsync returns false on second call, but assumes SQLite's locking.)

---

### **Finding 5: Endpoint ClaimsIdentity Construction Does Not Validate Email Consistency**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Api/Endpoints/InviteEndpoints.cs` (lines 37-44)

**Summary:** The endpoint constructs a ClaimsIdentity using `user.Email` (returned from AcceptAsync) and `googleEmail` (from ctx.User), but does not assert they match after AcceptAsync succeeds, even though AcceptAsync already validated the match.

**Failure Scenario:** If AcceptAsync is changed in the future to accept a user with a different email than the invitation (or if a bug is introduced), the cookie signed in line 45-47 could have an inconsistent email claim. This is low-risk because AcceptAsync performs the validation, but it violates defense-in-depth: the endpoint should assert the user.Email == googleEmail before signing in to prevent silent bugs if the service layer is modified incorrectly.

---

### **Finding 6: RecordConsumerAsync Has No Idempotency Check**
**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.DataAccess/Repositories/InvitationRepository.cs` (lines 109-112)

**Summary:** The UPDATE in `RecordConsumerAsync` has no WHERE clause protecting against re-execution with the same userId. Calling it twice for the same tokenHash will succeed both times, overwriting consumed_by_user_id with the same value.

**Failure Scenario:** If the transaction commit succeeds but the commit confirmation is lost (network failure), the retry loop in InvitationService might call RecordConsumerAsync again for the same invitation and userId. While this is idempotent in outcome (same userId written twice), it indicates the method is not transaction-safe if partial failures occur. A safer pattern would be `UPDATE ... WHERE consumed_by_user_id IS NULL` to detect if already recorded, or return rowsAffected for the caller to validate.

---

- **Finding 1:** Orphaned domain method (design/reuse)
- **Finding 2:** Missing integration test (quality/coverage)  
- **Finding 3:** Unchecked UPDATE result (efficiency/correctness)
- **Finding 4:** Race-condition verification gap (correctness)
- **Finding 5:** Missing defensive validation in endpoint (simplification/efficiency)
- **Finding 6:** Non-idempotent UPDATE for deferred operations (efficiency/correctness)

## Altitude-Level Code Review: PR #7 (US3 — Invitee Accepts Invitation)

I've completed the depth analysis of the four areas you flagged. Here are my findings:

---

### **FINDING 1: Polly Retry Count = 20 with Exponential Backoff Exponentially Exceeds Test Reality**

**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs`  
**Lines:** 27–39

**Summary:** MaxRetryAttempts=20 with exponential backoff (2^n * 50ms) + jitter creates a pathological worst-case delay of **~29 hours**, masking deeper design issues in a local SQLite test environment.

**Failure Scenario:** If a single retry loop genuinely exhausts all 20 attempts (which won't happen in the concurrent test because of the gate in line 162), the actual worst-case cumulative delay is 104.8 seconds (base) to 29 hours (with max jitter), far exceeding typical timeout thresholds. More critically: 20 retries is a band-aid for "SQLITE_BUSY + 20 concurrent requests" — the real solution is smarter SQLite tuning (WAL mode + timeout) or connection pooling, not retry avalanche. Once production adds 50+ concurrent requests, this silently becomes a denial-of-service vector in the service itself.

---

### **FINDING 2: KanbanWebAppFactory RemoveAll + Re-register Is Fragile Against Future Rate Limiter Policies**

**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/tests/integration/Infrastructure/KanbanWebAppFactory.cs`  
**Lines:** 62–83

**Summary:** `RemoveAll(typeof(IConfigureOptions<RateLimiterOptions>))` deletes ALL rate limiter configuration, then manually re-registers three policies ("anonymous", "authenticated", "mutating"). If a new rate limiter policy is added to Program.cs but not to the factory, tests will silently use defaults and fail unpredictably.

**Failure Scenario:** A future dev adds a fourth policy (e.g., "premium") to Program.cs at line 235+. The factory's RemoveAll still triggers and only re-registers the old three. Any integration test that hits an endpoint tagged with "premium" will silently use the ASP.NET Core defaults (not the factory overrides) and may fail under rate limits, while other tests pass. This is silent — no build error, just flaky tests. Better: Instead of RemoveAll + re-register, mutate only the specific policies you need to override (add a lambda in factory that tweaks existing limits post-registration).

---

### **FINDING 3: AcceptAsync Retry Safety — Confirmed Safe, But Fragile to Logic Changes**

**Files:** 
- `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Business/Services/InvitationService.cs` (lines 137–207)
- `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.DataAccess/Repositories/InvitationRepository.cs` (lines 78–100)

**Summary:** Your analysis is correct: TryConsumeAsync (line 162) performs an UPDATE WHERE consumed_at IS NULL, setting consumed_at to acceptedAt. If the UPDATE succeeds, rowsAffected==1 and it returns true. On retry attempt 2, consumed_at IS NOT NULL, so the WHERE fails, TryConsumeAsync returns false, and NotFoundException fires. Duplicate user creation is impossible. The retry is safe.

**Failure Scenario (Maintenance Risk):** This safety depends entirely on the WHERE clause in TryConsumeAsync remaining `consumed_at IS NULL`. If a future dev:
- Removes the IS NULL check (thinking "oh, idempotent, just set it again")
- Moves the TryConsumeAsync call outside the retry loop
- Changes newUserId assignment to happen once outside the loop (it currently regenerates per retry)

...then duplicate users become possible. The comment at line 158–161 explains the gate pattern, but the retail fragility is high. Better: Test explicitly for idempotence (run AcceptAsync twice with same token, expect NotFoundException on second call) so the contract is enforced.

---

### **FINDING 4: v1AuthGroup vs v1Group Split Is Subtle and Undocumented for Registrations**

**File:** `/Volumes/Work Drive/source/repos/kanban/src/Kanban.Api/Program.cs`  
**Lines:** 347–358

**Summary:** Two overlapping endpoint groups:
- `v1Group` (line 348–352): `RequireAuthorization("RegisteredUser")` — auth + must have user_id claim  
- `v1AuthGroup` (line 355–358): `RequireAuthorization()` — auth only, no user_id requirement  

The comment at line 354 explains the *why*, but there's no structural enforcement. InviteEndpoints.Map(v1Group) registers "issue invite" (needs RegisteredUser), while InviteEndpoints.MapAcceptEndpoint(v1AuthGroup) registers "accept invite" (doesn't need user_id). This is a convention, not a rule.

**Failure Scenario:** A future dev adds a new endpoint (e.g., "GET /invites/{id}") and accidentally calls `InviteEndpoints.MapNewEndpoint(v1AuthGroup)` instead of `v1Group`. The endpoint silently inherits weaker auth (only requires Google login, not RegisteredUser status), exposing data to unauthenticated invitees or other logged-in users. No compile error, no test failure unless you explicitly test that unregistered users cannot access it. Better: Rename groups to be more explicit (`v1RegisteredUserGroup`, `v1GoogleAuthOnlyGroup`) or use attribute-based routing (`.RequireAuthorization("RegisteredUser")` inline on each endpoint) so the auth requirement is visible at the endpoint level.

---

### Summary Table

| Finding | File | Lines | Risk Level | Category |
|---------|------|-------|-----------|----------|
| 1 | InvitationService.cs | 27–39 | **HIGH** | Masking design issue; retry avalanche in production |
| 2 | KanbanWebAppFactory.cs | 62–83 | **MEDIUM** | Silent test failures if future policies added |
| 3 | InvitationService.cs + InvitationRepository.cs | 137–207, 78–100 | **MEDIUM** | Correct now, but fragile to refactoring |
| 4 | Program.cs | 347–358 | **MEDIUM** | Convention-based auth; silent failures if misregistered |

**Recommendation:** Findings 1 and 4 should be addressed before merge. Findings 2 and 3 are good candidates for follow-up tasks to reduce future maintenance debt.

3. Inside AcceptAsync, at line 196: `tx.Commit()` is called
4. AcceptAsync returns the User object at line 199
5. Back in MapAcceptEndpoint at line 45-47: `ctx.SignInAsync()` is called AFTER AcceptAsync returns

The critical issue: AcceptAsync completes with a full transaction commit at line 196, then returns. SignInAsync is called at line 45-47 of the endpoint, which is OUTSIDE the AcceptAsync method and OUTSIDE the Polly retry policy. If SignInAsync throws, the user already exists in the DB but the response is 500 and unauthenticated.

However, SignInAsync exceptions would not be automatically retried by Polly because it's outside the RetryPolicy.ExecuteAsync() scope. The Polly retry only applies to database lock exceptions within AcceptAsync, not to authentication framework failures.

This is **CONFIRMED**.

---

- `TryConsumeAsync` (lines 78-100) calls ExecuteAsync and checks `rowsAffected == 1` (line 99)
- `RecordConsumerAsync` (lines 102-118) calls ExecuteAsync but does NOT check rowsAffected

1. Line 162: `TryConsumeAsync` is called - this marks consumed_at and returns false if the update affects 0 rows
2. Line 186: `RecordConsumerAsync` is called AFTER user insertion succeeds

- TryConsumeAsync succeeded (line 163 check), meaning the UPDATE found and modified a row
- The tokenHash is read again at line 168 via FindByTokenHashAsync immediately after
- RecordConsumerAsync uses the same tokenHash from the same transaction

This is **REFUTED** — lastSignInAt is already correctly typed as nullable.

content.text:
Good question — there are two separate concerns here. Let me break them down clearly.

---

## What you need in Google Cloud Console (all free)

1. **Create / select a project** — any free project works
2. **Enable the Google Identity (OAuth 2.0) API** — no cost
3. **Configure the OAuth Consent Screen**
   - User type: **External**
   - Status: **Testing** (no Google verification required; you add specific test accounts manually)
   - Add your own Gmail as a test user, plus any other accounts you'll sign in with during Playwright runs
4. **Create an OAuth 2.0 credential** (Credentials → Create → OAuth client ID → Web application)
   - Authorized redirect URIs:
     ```
     http://localhost:5077/signin-google
     https://localhost:7282/signin-google
     ```
   - Copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** → `dotnet user-secrets set` (already in your quickstart)
5. **No billing required** — the Google Identity API is free; "Testing" consent screen status means no quota limits apply to your listed test users

---

## The real problem: Google blocks automated sign-in

Even with valid credentials, Google's sign-in page uses reCAPTCHA and bot detection that will silently block Playwright. You can't automate `accounts.google.com` reliably.

**The standard solutions are:**

### Option A — Saved auth state (one manual login, reuse forever)
Playwright's `globalSetup` opens a real headed browser, you sign in manually once, it saves `playwright/.auth/admin.json`. Every test skips the Google page entirely by restoring that state.

- Pro: fully real auth flow, no code changes to the app
- Con: you re-run the setup whenever the Google session expires (~a week)

### Option B — Development-only auth bypass endpoint (recommended)
Add a `POST /api/v1/dev/authenticate` endpoint that only exists when `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development`. Playwright calls it with `{ email, role }` and gets back a real auth cookie — same one Google would have issued — without touching Google's servers.

- Pro: instant, no expiry, no manual steps, deterministic
- Con: adds ~20 lines to the API (but gated behind environment, never ships)

---

## My recommendation

**Option B** is what most teams building against Google OAuth actually do for e2e tests. It's what your `TestAuthenticationHandler` already does for integration tests — we'd just expose the same mechanism to Playwright over HTTP.

The Google Cloud Console setup (steps 1–5 above) is still worth doing so you can do a real manual demo sign-in. But for Playwright CI, the bypass endpoint is the reliable path.

Want me to implement Option B (the dev bypass endpoint + Playwright global setup), or would you prefer to go with Option A (saved state)?
the first authorized uri is waht goes in authorized javascript origins I assume, why is it not https?

content.thinking:
The user is asking about the authorized JavaScript origins in Google Cloud Console. Let me clarify:

1. **Authorized JavaScript Origins** - these are the origins from which JavaScript can make requests to Google APIs. For OAuth 2.0, this is used when you're making OAuth requests from the browser using the Google Identity Services library. However, for server-side OAuth (which is what ASP.NET Core OIDC middleware does), JavaScript Origins aren't actually needed.

2. **Authorized Redirect URIs** - these are the URIs where Google sends the authentication response after the user signs in. This IS what matters for ASP.NET Core's OIDC middleware.


3. **Why both HTTP and HTTPS redirect URIs are configured** - Development mode in ASP.NET Core doesn't enforce HTTPS redirection, and Google explicitly allows `http://localhost` for development purposes as an exception to their HTTPS requirement. The HTTPS variant is also registered because the app uses HTTPS when running normally outside of development mode.

For the JavaScript origins question, I need to clarify the distinction: **Authorized JavaScript Origins** are only needed when using Google's client-side JavaScript libraries (like the Sign-In button), but ASP.NET Core uses server-side OIDC authentication, so this field isn't required. **Authorized Redirect URIs** is what actually matters here—that's the callback endpoint where Google sends the authorization code.

content.text:
Two separate fields to clarify:

**Authorized JavaScript Origins** — only needed if you're using the Google Identity Services *JavaScript library* (the browser-side Google Sign-In button). Your app uses ASP.NET Core's server-side OIDC middleware, so this field is **not required at all**. Leave it empty.

**Authorized Redirect URIs** — this is the one that matters. It's the callback URL Google POST's the auth code back to after the user signs in. That's what you need:
```
http://localhost:5077/signin-google
https://localhost:7282/signin-google
```

---

**Why HTTP for localhost?**

Google makes a specific exception: `http://localhost` (and `http://127.0.0.1`) are allowed as redirect URIs even though Google normally requires HTTPS everywhere. They do this precisely for local development — you'd otherwise need a self-signed cert or a tunnel just to test OAuth.

In your app it's also consistent: `Program.cs` only enables `app.UseHttpsRedirection()` when `!IsDevelopment()`, so the dev server runs on HTTP at port 5077. The HTTPS port (7282) is there if you run with the dev cert, but the HTTP one is the typical local dev path.

So in Google Cloud Console, just add both to **Authorized Redirect URIs**, leave **Authorized JavaScript Origins** blank, and you're set.

Both together is the right call. Here's what I'd recommend:

---

## The architecture: one test suite, two auth paths

The Playwright tests themselves are **identical** in both cases. Only `globalSetup` switches paths based on an environment variable:

```
PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS=true  →  CI path: calls dev bypass endpoint, gets cookie instantly
(env var absent)             →  Demo path: restores saved storageState from real Google login
```

```
CI pipeline
  └── PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS=true
  └── globalSetup hits POST /api/v1/dev/authenticate → saves playwright/.auth/admin.json
  └── all tests run using that state

Local demo
  └── run setup script once: npx playwright test --project=setup (opens headed browser)
  └── you sign in to Google manually → saved to playwright/.auth/admin.json
  └── npx playwright test --headed runs the full real flow
```

---

## What needs to be built

1. **`POST /api/v1/dev/authenticate`** — Development-only endpoint, accepts `{ email }`, issues a real auth cookie without touching Google. ~20 lines.

2. **`playwright/globalSetup.ts`** — checks `PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS`. If true, calls the bypass endpoint. If false, runs a headed browser login against real Google and saves state.

3. **`playwright/auth.setup.ts`** — the manual Google sign-in project (only used locally for the demo path).

4. **`playwright.config.ts`** — wire the two projects up: `setup` (demo only) and the main test suite.

---

## Package scripts

```json
"test:e2e"       : "PLAYWRIGHT_AUTH_BYPASS=true playwright test",
"test:e2e:demo"  : "playwright test --headed",
"test:e2e:setup" : "playwright test --project=setup"
```

---
